column1: Perfusion
column2: Continuous adequate circulation through capillaries that delivers oxygen and nutrients to cells and removes metabolic waste.

column1: What is the fundamental purpose of emergency care in terms of cellular physiology?
column2: Restore or sustain adequate perfusion so cells receive oxygen, glucose and other necessary substances and metabolic wastes are removed.

column1: What pathophysiology competency do the National EMS Education Standards identify for EMTs?
column2: Apply the pathophysiology of respiration and perfusion to patient assessment and management.

column1: Cellular metabolism (cellular respiration)
column2: The breakdown of fuel molecules to produce energy for cellular functions.

column1: What is the primary metabolic fuel discussed in Chapter 8?
column2: Glucose.

column1: Aerobic Metabolism
column2: Cellular chemical and physical processes that generate energy in the presence of oxygen.

column1: Glycolysis
column2: The breakdown of glucose into pyruvic acid in the cytosol, yielding a small amount of ATP.

column1: Does glycolysis require oxygen?
column2: No.

column1: Where does glycolysis occur?
column2: In the cytosol, not the mitochondria.

column1: ATP
column2: Adenosine triphosphate; the energy source used for cellular functions such as muscle contraction and active transport.

column1: What happens to glycolysis products when oxygen is available?
column2: Mitochondrial pathways use them to generate much larger amounts of ATP.

column1: What is oxygen's role in mitochondrial energy production?
column2: It serves as the terminal electron acceptor in the electron transport chain.

column1: What are the principal products of aerobic metabolism besides ATP?
column2: Heat, carbon dioxide and water.

column1: How does metabolic heat affect the body?
column2: It helps maintain core body temperature; increased metabolism can increase core temperature.

column1: How is metabolic carbon dioxide eliminated?
column2: Blood carries it to the lungs, where it is exhaled.

column1: How may increased metabolic CO₂ production affect breathing?
column2: It can increase respiratory rate to facilitate CO₂ removal.

column1: What happens to water produced during aerobic metabolism?
column2: It is reused or excreted.

column1: Anaerobic Metabolism
column2: Cellular energy-producing processes that occur without adequate oxygen for oxidative metabolism.

column1: How does glycolysis continue during inadequate oxidative metabolism?
column2: Pyruvate is converted to lactate, allowing glycolysis to continue.

column1: Why is anaerobic metabolism insufficient to sustain normal cellular function indefinitely?
column2: It produces much less ATP than aerobic metabolism.

column1: Where does conversion of pyruvate to lactate occur?
column2: In the cytosol.

column1: Does an elevated lactate level necessarily prove cellular hypoxia?
column2: No. Lactate can also be produced in the presence of oxygen and reused as fuel.

column1: Why can severe oxygen-delivery failure cause cellular death?
column2: Energy depletion and acidosis impair enzymes, disrupt membranes and contribute to cellular injury and death.

column1: Is lactate alone responsible for acidosis and cell death during inadequate oxygen delivery?
column2: No; multiple mechanisms contribute.

column1: Where is sodium (Na⁺) predominantly concentrated?
column2: Outside cells, in extracellular fluid.

column1: Where is potassium (K⁺) predominantly concentrated?
column2: Inside cells, in intracellular fluid.

column1: What functions depend on sodium and potassium concentration gradients?
column2: Nerve impulse transmission and muscle contraction.

column1: In which direction do substances tend to move along a concentration gradient?
column2: From higher to lower concentration.

column1: Why is active transport required to maintain sodium and potassium gradients?
column2: The pump moves both ions against their respective concentration gradients.

column1: Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (sodium–potassium pump)
column2: A protein in the cell membrane lipid bilayer that uses ATP to transport sodium out of the cell and potassium into it.

column1: How many sodium and potassium ions move during one sodium–potassium pump ATP cycle?
column2: Three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in.

column1: What is the first step of the sodium–potassium pump cycle?
column2: Intracellular sodium binds to the pump.

column1: What happens to ATP after sodium binds to the sodium–potassium pump?
column2: ATP transfers a phosphate to the pump, leaving ADP.

column1: How does the sodium–potassium pump release sodium?
column2: Phosphorylation changes its shape, closing the intracellular side and opening the extracellular side.

column1: What happens when extracellular potassium binds to the sodium–potassium pump?
column2: The phosphate detaches.

column1: How is potassium released into the cell by the sodium–potassium pump?
column2: The extracellular side closes and the intracellular side opens, releasing potassium into the cell.

column1: What can deplete ATP and impair sodium–potassium pump function?
column2: Inadequate perfusion, oxygen delivery or glucose delivery.

column1: Why does ATP depletion cause cellular swelling?
column2: The sodium–potassium pump fails, sodium accumulates inside the cell, and water follows.

column1: What may happen if cellular swelling progresses severely?
column2: Cell membranes may rupture and the cell may die.

column1: How can widespread cellular injury affect organ function?
column2: It can cause organ failure.

column1: What are the 11 components of the physiological chain of perfusion?
column2: Ambient air composition; patent airway; ventilation mechanics; ventilation regulation; V/Q ratio; blood gas transport; blood volume; myocardial pump function; SVR; microcirculation; blood pressure.

column1: What two circulatory factors are necessary for pulmonary capillary perfusion?
column2: Adequate venous volume and right ventricular pump function.

column1: Why must ventilation, gas exchange, circulation and cellular metabolism work together?
column2: Failure at any link can reduce oxygen delivery or waste removal and ultimately decrease ATP production.

column1: What blood and circulatory factors support effective tissue gas exchange?
column2: Adequate hemoglobin and plasma, cardiac output and vascular tone, together with effective capillary exchange.

column1: What are the foundational EMT responsibilities when perfusion is threatened?
column2: Assessment, oxygenation and ventilation, bleeding control, reassessment and transport.

column1: What determines whether an EMT is authorized to perform a skill?
column2: State law, training, licensure, credentialing, agency protocols and medical direction.

column1: Does understanding an intervention or reading a national guideline authorize an EMT to perform it?
column2: No. Local authorization and medical direction determine scope.

column1: What should an EMT evaluate when identifying a disrupted link in the perfusion chain?
column2: Scene hazards and reversible BLS problems, airway patency, ventilation, gas exchange, oxygen content, blood flow and cellular utilization as appropriate.

column1: Is the perfusion chain a fixed treatment sequence?
column2: No; it is a clinical reasoning framework.

column1: What should an EMT do when additional capabilities are needed?
column2: Request them early while continuing indicated BLS care, reassessment and transport.

column1: What is normal atmospheric pressure at sea level in the chapter?
column2: Approximately 760 mmHg.

column1: Partial pressure of a gas
column2: The portion of total gas pressure contributed by that gas, proportional to its concentration.

column1: What percentage of ambient air is oxygen at sea level?
column2: 20.95%, approximately 21%.

column1: What is oxygen's partial pressure in ambient air at sea level in the chapter's table?
column2: 159.2 mmHg.

column1: What percentage of ambient air is nitrogen?
column2: 78.08%, approximately 78%.

column1: What is nitrogen's partial pressure at sea level in the chapter's table?
column2: 593.4 mmHg.

column1: What percentage of ambient air is argon?
column2: 0.93%, approximately 0.9%.

column1: What is argon's partial pressure in the chapter's ambient air table?
column2: 7.1 mmHg.

column1: What is the carbon dioxide concentration in the chapter's ambient air table?
column2: 0.03% in the chapter's illustrative atmospheric composition table.

column1: What is the carbon dioxide partial pressure in the chapter's ambient air table?
column2: 0.2 mmHg, based on the chapter's listed concentration.

column1: What combined concentration and partial pressure do the gases listed in the chapter's table represent?
column2: 99.99% and 759.9 mmHg; trace gases account for the remainder.

column1: FiO₂ (fraction of inspired oxygen)
column2: The fraction of oxygen inhaled, expressed as a decimal rather than a percentage.

column1: What is the FiO₂ of ambient air?
column2: Approximately 0.21.

column1: What FiO₂ represents 100% oxygen?
What approximate FiO₂ does the chapter give for a nonrebreather mask?
column2: 0.95; actual concentration depends on fit, flow, reservoir inflation, demand and leaks.

column1: FDO₂ (fraction of delivered oxygen)
column2: The oxygen fraction delivered by a ventilation device; FiO₂ is commonly used in its place.

column1: What approximate FDO₂ does the chapter give for a BVM with reservoir at 15 L/min?
column2: 0.95–0.98 under suitable conditions; not a guaranteed concentration.

column1: What factors affect oxygen concentration actually delivered by a mask or BVM?
column2: Mask fit, reservoir inflation, gas flow, patient inspiratory demand and leaks.

column1: Why should EMTs not rely solely on theoretical oxygen delivery concentrations?
column2: Actual performance varies; assess the clinical response and adequacy of ventilation.

column1: How can enclosed-space fire gases cause hypoxia by displacement?
column2: They displace available oxygen, reducing inspired oxygen.

column1: How does carbon monoxide impair oxygen transport?
column2: It binds to the oxygen-carrying portion of red blood cells, impairing oxygen delivery.

column1: How does cyanide cause cellular hypoxia?
column2: It prevents cells from utilizing oxygen even when alveolar and blood oxygen levels are adequate.

column1: Why can standard pulse oximetry be misleading in carbon monoxide poisoning?
column2: It cannot reliably distinguish carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin.

column1: What is the BLS implication of a reassuring SpO₂ reading in suspected carbon monoxide poisoning?
column2: Do not exclude poisoning or delay appropriate oxygen and transport; consider exposure history and clinical findings.

column1: What is the scene-safety priority in suspected toxic atmospheric exposure?
column2: Do not enter an unsafe atmosphere; coordinate with appropriate fire/hazmat personnel.

column1: Patent Airway
column2: An airway that is open and clear of obstructions.

column1: What substances or structures can obstruct an airway?
column2: Blood, secretions, vomitus, swollen tissues, bone, teeth, tongue or foreign material.

column1: What are the airway obstruction sites in superior-to-inferior order in the chapter?
column2: Nasopharynx, oropharynx, posterior pharynx, epiglottis, larynx, trachea, bronchi and bronchioles.

column1: Nasopharynx
column2: The portion of the pharynx extending from the posterior nasal cavity to the soft palate.

column1: How can fluid or blood in the nasopharynx impair breathing?
column2: It can drain into the pharynx and be aspirated.

column1: When may the nasopharynx provide an alternative airway?
column2: When the mandible is fractured or the teeth are clenched.

column1: Why is nasal airway patency particularly important in infants?
column2: Infants preferentially breathe through the nose, though they are not invariably unable to mouth-breathe.

column1: Oropharynx
column2: The central pharynx between the soft palate and epiglottis, with the mouth as its opening.

column1: What can obstruct the oropharynx?
column2: Tongue, foreign bodies, swelling, hematomas, blood or vomitus.

column1: How does aspiration of liquid into alveoli affect respiration?
column2: It can impair gas exchange.

column1: Epiglottis
column2: A leaf-shaped cartilaginous flap behind the root of the tongue that covers the laryngeal opening during swallowing.

column1: What can cause the epiglottis to obstruct the airway?
column2: Inflammation or swelling, or displacement toward the glottic opening when tongue muscles relax.

column1: What basic airway maneuvers may lift a displaced epiglottis away from the glottic opening?
column2: Jaw-thrust or chin-lift, as appropriate to the patient's circumstances.

column1: Larynx
column2: The structure between the pharynx and trachea that contains the vocal cords.

column1: What is the narrowest point of the adult laryngeal airway according to the chapter's traditional model?
column2: The vocal cords.

column1: How should the traditional description of the cricoid as always the narrowest point in children younger than eight be understood?
column2: It is an oversimplification; narrowest dimensions vary with age, anatomy and measurement, though the nondistensible cricoid remains important.

column1: Why is airway swelling especially consequential in children?
column2: Their airways have a small caliber.

column1: Laryngeal Spasm
column2: Also called laryngospasm; contraction of the vocal cords that closes the airway and prevents air from entering the trachea.

column1: What may trigger laryngospasm according to the chapter?
column2: Injury, airway insertion or medications.

column1: How can a laryngeal fracture obstruct the airway?
column2: The fractured structure may collapse inward.

column1: Trachea
column2: The tube leading from the larynx toward the lungs.

column1: Carina
column2: The point where the trachea divides into the right and left mainstem bronchi.

column1: What surface landmarks approximate the location of the carina in the chapter?
column2: Second intercostal space/angle of Louis anteriorly; T4 posteriorly.

column1: Bronchi
column2: The two main branches of the trachea that conduct air to the lungs; singular: bronchus.

column1: Bronchioles
column2: Small branches of the bronchi; distal bronchioles lack cartilaginous rings and contain smooth muscle.

column1: Alveoli
column2: The air sacs of the lungs where gas exchange occurs; singular: alveolus.

column1: How does bronchitis increase airway resistance?
column2: Inflammation of the bronchial mucous lining reduces airway diameter.

column1: How does asthma obstruct airflow?
column2: Airway inflammation and smooth muscle contraction narrow the airways.

column1: Bronchoconstriction
column2: Contraction of airway smooth muscle that narrows the airway and increases resistance.

column1: Why does asthma cause wheezing?
column2: Narrowed airways produce turbulent airflow.

column1: What is an early expiratory finding in asthma described in the chapter?
column2: Prolonged exhalation.

column1: What gas-exchange problems may develop with asthma?
column2: Hypoxia and carbon dioxide retention (hypercarbia).

column1: Hypercarbia (hypercapnia)
column2: Elevated carbon dioxide.

column1: Does a patent airway alone establish adequate ventilation or protection against aspiration?
column2: No.

column1: Ventilation
column2: The mechanical movement of air into and out of the lungs, primarily through changes in intrathoracic pressure.

column1: What structures bound the thoracic cavity superiorly?
column2: Neck muscles and ribs 1–2.

column1: What forms the inferior boundary of the thoracic cavity?
column2: The diaphragm.

column1: What forms the anterior boundary of the thoracic cavity?
column2: Muscles, ribs and sternum.

column1: What forms the posterior boundary of the thoracic cavity?
column2: Muscles, vertebrae and ribs.

column1: What separates the right and left hemithorax?
column2: The mediastinum.

column1: Boyle’s Law
column2: At constant temperature, gas pressure is inversely proportional to gas volume.

column1: How does Boyle's law explain inhalation?
column2: Thoracic expansion lowers pressure below atmospheric pressure so air enters.

column1: How does Boyle's law explain exhalation?
column2: Reduced thoracic volume raises pressure above atmospheric pressure so air exits.

column1: Is normal inhalation active or passive?
column2: Active; respiratory muscles contract.

column1: What proportion of inspiratory effort does the diaphragm provide according to the chapter?
column2: Approximately 60–70%.

column1: How does the diaphragm move during inhalation?
column2: It contracts and descends, increasing thoracic volume.

column1: How do the external intercostals contribute to inhalation?
column2: They lift the ribs upward and outward.

column1: What pressure change illustrates inhalation in the chapter?
column2: A decrease from 760 to 758 mmHg; illustrative, not a fixed physiological value.

column1: Is normal exhalation active or passive?
column2: Normally passive, through muscle relaxation and elastic recoil.

column1: What pressure illustrates exhalation in the chapter?
column2: 762 mmHg; an illustrative value rather than a fixed pressure.

column1: What is the function of serous fluid between the visceral and parietal pleura?
column2: It couples lung movement to the chest wall, opposing elastic recoil and maintaining negative intrapleural pressure.

column1: How does the sternocleidomastoid assist inhalation?
column2: It lifts the sternum.

column1: How do the scalene muscles assist inhalation?
column2: They elevate ribs 1 and 2.

column1: How does the pectoralis minor assist inhalation?
column2: It elevates ribs 3–5.

column1: How do abdominal muscles assist active exhalation?
column2: They raise abdominal pressure and push the diaphragm upward.

column1: How do internal intercostals assist active exhalation?
column2: They pull the sternum and ribs downward.

column1: How do accessory inspiratory muscles increase ventilation?
column2: They increase thoracic volume and negative pressure.

column1: How do accessory expiratory muscles increase ventilation?
column2: They decrease thoracic volume and increase pressure, making exhalation active.

column1: In what chronic lung conditions may exhalation become active?
column2: COPD, including emphysema.

column1: Why can sustained accessory muscle use lead to respiratory failure?
column2: Extra work consumes energy; inadequate oxygen or fuel can cause respiratory muscle fatigue.

column1: Compliance
column2: The ability of the chest wall and lungs to stretch, distend and expand.

column1: What conditions can impair effective lung or chest-wall expansion?
column2: Pneumonia, pulmonary edema, a flail segment or neuromuscular disease.

column1: Airway Resistance
column2: Opposition to airflow through conducting airways, related to airway diameter.

column1: What is the relationship between airway diameter and airway resistance?
column2: Reduced diameter increases resistance.

column1: What are common causes of increased airway resistance?
column2: Edema, mucus and bronchoconstriction; the chapter identifies edema as the most common cause.

column1: What illustrative pressures show the pleural pressure gradient in the chapter?
column2: 760 mmHg outside the chest, 758 mmHg in the lung and 754 mmHg in the pleural space; not fixed values.

column1: How can an open chest wound cause pneumothorax?
column2: A break in the parietal pleura allows air into the pleural space.

column1: How can lung injury cause pneumothorax?
column2: A break in the visceral pleura permits air to enter the pleural space.

column1: Why can a pneumothorax cause lung collapse?
column2: Pleural air disrupts coupling between the lung and chest wall.

column1: How can tension pneumothorax lead to shock?
column2: It impairs lung expansion and venous return, producing obstructive shock.

column1: What chest-seal limitation does the chapter's updated 2024 guidance identify?
column2: A vented seal may be considered for a spontaneously breathing patient with open pneumothorax; the cited statement advises against seals in open pneumothorax receiving PPV. Follow local protocols.

column1: What findings should prompt concern for worsening pneumothorax during BLS care?
column2: Worsening distress, asymmetric breath sounds or signs of shock.

column1: What should EMTs prioritize if a chest trauma patient requires ventilation?
column2: Continue needed ventilation, follow local chest-wound protocols and avoid delaying transport.

column1: Tidal Volume (VT)
column2: The amount of air moved into and out of the lungs in one breath.

column1: Frequency of Ventilation (f)
column2: The number of ventilations in one minute.

column1: Minute Ventilation (Minute Volume)
column2: The total volume of air moved into and out of the lungs in one minute.

column1: What is the formula for minute ventilation?
column2: Tidal volume × respiratory frequency.

column1: What is minute ventilation at a tidal volume of 500 mL and rate of 12/min?
column2: 6,000 mL/min (6 L/min).

column1: Dead Air Space (VD)
column2: Conducting airway areas outside the alveoli where inhaled air collects but gas exchange does not occur.

column1: Which airways are examples of anatomical dead space?
column2: Trachea, bronchi and bronchioles.

column1: What is average adult anatomical dead space in the chapter's example?
column2: Approximately 150 mL.

column1: Why does exhaled air still contain approximately 17–18% oxygen?
column2: Some inspired air remains in conducting airway dead space and does not participate in gas exchange.

column1: Alveolar Ventilation
column2: The amount of inspired air reaching the gas-exchanging alveoli; expressed per minute when calculated as alveolar minute ventilation.

column1: What is the formula for alveolar minute ventilation?
column2: (Tidal volume − dead-space volume) × respiratory frequency.

column1: What is alveolar minute ventilation for a tidal volume of 500 mL, dead space of 150 mL and rate of 12/min?
column2: 4,200 mL/min (4.2 L/min).

column1: What is minute ventilation for a tidal volume of 200 mL and rate of 28/min?
column2: 5,600 mL/min (5.6 L/min).

column1: What is alveolar minute ventilation for tidal volume 200 mL, dead space 150 mL and rate 28/min?
column2: 1,400 mL/min (1.4 L/min).

column1: Why can rapid shallow breathing produce near-normal minute ventilation but inadequate alveolar ventilation?
column2: Dead space consumes a larger proportion of each small breath, so little fresh air reaches alveoli.

column1: What is the effect of low alveolar ventilation on carbon dioxide?
column2: CO₂ retention, with possible impairment of oxygenation.

column1: Why is supplemental oxygen alone insufficient for inadequate ventilation?
column2: It does not correct inadequate movement of air into and out of alveoli; assisted ventilation may be needed.

column1: Does visible chest rise quantify alveolar ventilation?
column2: No.

column1: What very rapid respiratory rates illustrate potentially unsustainable breathing in the chapter?
column2: Adults ≥40/min and children >60/min; teaching examples, not universal failure cutoffs.

column1: Why can extremely rapid respiratory rates contribute to respiratory fatigue?
column2: They reduce filling time and may increase work of breathing.

column1: What is the BLS priority when ventilation is inadequate?
column2: Provide appropriate assisted ventilation without waiting for ALS.

column1: How can excessive positive-pressure ventilation adversely affect circulation?
column2: Increased intrathoracic pressure can reduce venous return and preload, especially in hypovolemia.

column1: Why should adequate exhalation be allowed between assisted breaths?
column2: Incomplete exhalation and air trapping may worsen intrathoracic pressure and impair ventilation or circulation.

column1: Respiratory Control Centers
column2: Brainstem centers that regulate breathing, including the dorsal and ventral respiratory groups and pontine respiratory center.

column1: What brainstem structures regulate respiration in the chapter's model?
column2: Medulla and pons, including DRG, VRG, central chemoreceptors, apneustic center and pneumotaxic center.

column1: What peripheral sensory structures participate in respiratory regulation?
column2: Carotid and aortic bodies and lung stretch, irritant and J-receptors.

column1: Which nerve supplies the diaphragm in the respiratory-control diagram?
column2: Phrenic nerve.

column1: What other peripheral nerves are included in the respiratory-control model?
column2: Intercostal nerves; the vagus nerve is associated with the dorsal respiratory group in the chapter's diagram.

column1: Chemoreceptors
column2: Receptors that monitor oxygen, carbon dioxide and pH and stimulate changes in respiratory rate and depth.

column1: Central Chemoreceptors
column2: Medullary receptors especially sensitive to carbon dioxide and cerebrospinal fluid pH.

column1: How does increased CO₂ stimulate central chemoreceptors?
column2: CO₂ combines with water to form carbonic acid, increasing hydrogen ions and lowering pH; breathing rate and depth increase.

column1: Peripheral Chemoreceptors
column2: Receptors in the aortic arch and carotid bodies especially sensitive to falling arterial oxygen, also responding to CO₂ and pH.

column1: What ventilatory response follows significant arterial oxygen reduction detected by peripheral chemoreceptors?
column2: Increased respiratory rate and depth.

column1: Hypercapnic (hypercarbic) drive
column2: The normal ventilatory stimulation associated with increased CO₂ and related pH changes.

column1: What is the traditional hypoxic-drive model in chronic COPD?
column2: It proposes that chronic CO₂ elevation reduces central chemoreceptor responsiveness, making low oxygen more influential; this is an oversimplification, not a universal switch.

column1: Does COPD universally change respiratory control from CO₂ to oxygen alone?
column2: No.

column1: Why can excessive oxygen worsen hypercapnia in some COPD patients?
column2: Altered V/Q matching, the Haldane effect and changes in ventilation can contribute.

column1: Haldane effect (as relevant to oxygen-induced hypercapnia)
column2: Oxygenated hemoglobin carries less CO₂.

column1: What oxygen saturation target does the chapter identify for patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure?
column2: Commonly 88–92%, subject to presentation and local guidance; never withhold needed oxygen or ventilation from a critically hypoxemic or failing patient.

column1: What does the chapter's COPD evidence clarification say about titrated oxygen versus indiscriminate high-flow oxygen?
column2: A prehospital randomized trial found better outcomes with titrated oxygen in suspected COPD exacerbation; urgent oxygenation and ventilation needs still take priority.

column1: Irritant Receptors
column2: Airway receptors sensitive to irritating gases, aerosols and particles.

column1: What responses result from stimulation of irritant receptors?
column2: Cough, bronchoconstriction and increased ventilatory rate.

column1: Stretch Receptors
column2: Airway smooth-muscle receptors that monitor lung size and volume.

column1: How do stretch receptors protect against overinflation?
column2: High tidal volumes stimulate a reduction in ventilation rate and volume.

column1: J-receptors
column2: Receptors near the alveolar capillaries that respond to increases in capillary pressure.

column1: What breathing pattern results from J-receptor stimulation?
column2: Rapid, shallow ventilation.

column1: Dorsal Respiratory Group (DRG)
column2: A respiratory control group in the posterior medulla involved in normal quiet breathing and relaying sensory information about rate and depth.

column1: Ventral Respiratory Group (VRG)
column2: A respiratory group in the anterior medulla containing inspiratory and expiratory neurons and participating in increased ventilatory effort.

column1: What is the role of the VRG during forced breathing in the chapter's model?
column2: Inspiratory neurons recruit inspiratory accessory muscles; expiratory neurons activate expiratory accessory muscles.

column1: How should the chapter's assertion that the VRG is the sole source of respiratory motor impulses be treated?
column2: As a simplified model whose exclusivity is not established in the supplied source.

column1: Pontine Respiratory Center
column2: Also called the pneumotaxic center; a center in the pons that inhibits inspiratory activity to help transition to exhalation.

column1: What inspiratory and expiratory timing illustrates the chapter's respiratory cycle?
column2: Two seconds of inspiration followed by three seconds of expiration, yielding 12 breaths/min; illustrative timing.

column1: Ventilation/Perfusion (V/Q) Ratio
column2: The relationship between alveolar ventilation (V, L/min) and pulmonary capillary blood flow (Q, L/min).

column1: External respiration
column2: Gas exchange between alveoli and pulmonary capillaries: blood gains oxygen and releases carbon dioxide.

column1: Internal respiration
column2: Gas exchange between systemic capillaries and cells through interstitial fluid: cells gain oxygen and release carbon dioxide.

column1: How do alveoli at the lung apex differ from those at the base in the chapter's gravity model?
column2: Apical alveoli are larger and less compliant with higher surface tension; basal alveoli are more compliant.

column1: Why does the lung apex have relatively wasted ventilation?
column2: Blood flow is relatively low compared with ventilation.

column1: Where are ventilation and perfusion greatest in the chapter's upright lung model?
column2: At the bases of the lungs.

column1: Why is there relatively wasted perfusion at the lung bases?
column2: Perfusion exceeds ventilation there.

column1: What overall normal V/Q relationship is described in the chapter?
column2: Less than 1.

column1: What can occur if alveolar pressure exceeds pulmonary capillary pressure?
column2: Local capillary flow may stop, compromising gas exchange and contributing to hypoxemia and hypoxia.

column1: How can severe blood loss contribute to pulmonary perfusion problems?
column2: Reduced blood pressure and blood flow can compromise pulmonary capillary perfusion.

column1: What is a ventilatory V/Q disturbance?
column2: Perfusion reaches alveoli with inadequate ventilation; blood flow is relatively wasted.

column1: How does asthma create a ventilatory V/Q disturbance?
column2: Airway narrowing reduces ventilation to perfused alveoli.

column1: What BLS treatment principles address asthma-related ventilation problems?
column2: Support oxygenation and ventilation as indicated; bronchodilators only when authorized by local protocol.

column1: What is a perfusion V/Q disturbance?
column2: Ventilation reaches alveoli with inadequate blood flow; ventilation is relatively wasted.

column1: How can arterial hemorrhage contribute to wasted ventilation and tissue hypoxia?
column2: Blood loss reduces pulmonary perfusion, circulating blood volume and oxygen-carrying capacity.

column1: What is the BLS priority for a hemorrhage-related perfusion disturbance?
column2: Control bleeding, support oxygenation and ventilation as indicated, and expedite definitive care; oxygen alone does not replace blood or circulation.

column1: What drives oxygen and carbon dioxide diffusion at the lungs and tissues?
column2: Partial-pressure gradients, from higher to lower partial pressure.

column1: What approximate oxygen transport rate does the chapter give?
column2: Approximately 1,000 mL/min; a chapter teaching value.

column1: What percentage of transported oxygen is bound to hemoglobin in the chapter?
column2: Approximately 97–98.5%.

column1: What percentage of oxygen is dissolved in plasma in the chapter?
column2: Approximately 1.5–3%; insufficient to sustain life alone.

column1: How many oxygen-binding sites does hemoglobin have?
column2: Four.

column1: What hemoglobin saturation corresponds to one, two, three and four occupied oxygen-binding sites?
column2: 25%, 50%, 75% and 100%, respectively, for that molecule.

column1: How does binding one oxygen molecule influence additional oxygen binding to hemoglobin?
column2: It increases affinity for the remaining sites.

column1: Oxyhemoglobin
column2: Hemoglobin with at least one oxygen molecule attached.

column1: Deoxyhemoglobin
column2: Hemoglobin without oxygen molecules attached.

column1: Why can an anemic patient have normal SpO₂ despite impaired tissue oxygen delivery?
column2: Saturation reflects the proportion of measurable hemoglobin carrying oxygen, not the total amount of hemoglobin.

column1: Does supplemental oxygen replace missing hemoglobin in anemia?
column2: No; oxygen may be appropriate for hypoxemia, respiratory distress or critical illness according to protocol, not solely because anemia is suspected.

column1: What factors may impair pulse oximetry reliability?
column2: Motion, poor peripheral perfusion and dyshemoglobinemia.

column1: What does pulse oximetry estimate?
column2: Arterial oxygen saturation (SpO₂); it does not establish adequate ventilation, hemoglobin concentration or tissue perfusion.

column1: Should a reassuring pulse oximeter reading override signs of respiratory distress?
column2: No. Assess the clinical findings and trends rather than relying on saturation alone.

column1: What percentage of carbon dioxide is transported as bicarbonate?
column2: Approximately 70%.

column1: Where is bicarbonate formed for CO₂ transport and where is the reaction reversed?
column2: Formed in red blood cells, carried in plasma and converted back in the lungs.

column1: What percentage of CO₂ is transported on hemoglobin?
column2: Approximately 23%.

column1: What percentage of CO₂ is transported dissolved in plasma?
column2: Approximately 7%.

column1: Which direction does oxygen diffuse during alveolar gas exchange?
column2: From alveoli into pulmonary capillaries.

column1: Which direction does carbon dioxide diffuse during alveolar gas exchange?
column2: From pulmonary capillaries into alveoli for exhalation.

column1: Where does oxygenated pulmonary blood travel next?
column2: To the left heart and then the body.

column1: Which direction does oxygen diffuse during tissue gas exchange?
column2: From systemic capillaries toward cells.

column1: Which direction does carbon dioxide diffuse during tissue gas exchange?
column2: From cells toward systemic capillaries, then via the right heart to the lungs.

column1: What approximate blood volume per kilogram is used in the chapter?
column2: 70 mL/kg.

column1: What estimated blood volume does the chapter give for a 70 kg (154 lb) adult?
What are the two major components of blood by approximate volume?
column2: Plasma 55%; formed elements 45%.

column1: What proportion of plasma is water?
column2: Approximately 91%.

column1: What is the main role of albumin in plasma fluid balance?
column2: It contributes to plasma oncotic pressure.

column1: What is the function of plasma antibodies?
column2: Immunity.

column1: What plasma protein is identified as a major clotting factor in the chapter?
column2: Fibrinogen.

column1: What are the three categories of formed elements in blood?
column2: Red blood cells (erythrocytes), white blood cells (leukocytes) and platelets (thrombocytes).

column1: What approximate red-cell volume percentages are listed for men and women?
column2: 48% in men and 42% in women; approximate chapter values.

column1: What are platelets (thrombocytes)?
column2: Cell fragments involved in blood clotting.

column1: Which vascular system serves as the major blood reservoir?
column2: The venous capacitance system.

What percentage of blood is in the arterial system in the chapter's distribution model?
What percentage of blood is in pulmonary vessels in the chapter's distribution model?

Hydrostatic Pressure
column2: The push exerted by blood against vessel walls that tends to drive fluid out of capillaries.

column1: How can elevated capillary hydrostatic pressure cause edema?
column2: It increases outward fluid movement from capillaries.

column1: How can left ventricular failure lead to pulmonary edema?
column2: Blood backs up into pulmonary capillaries, increasing hydrostatic pressure and fluid movement into lung tissues.

column1: Plasma Oncotic Pressure
column2: Also called colloid oncotic pressure; the pull created by plasma proteins such as albumin that opposes capillary fluid filtration.

column1: How may low albumin contribute to edema?
column2: Reduced oncotic pressure allows greater fluid filtration out of capillaries.

column1: Does high plasma oncotic pressure alone establish fluid overload?
column2: No.

column1: Does low albumin with edema necessarily prove intravascular volume depletion?
column2: No.

column1: What other factors influence capillary fluid exchange besides hydrostatic and oncotic pressure?
column2: Capillary permeability, interstitial pressures and lymphatic drainage.

column1: Cardiac Output
column2: The volume of blood ejected by the left ventricle per minute.

column1: What is the approximate resting adult cardiac output in the chapter?
column2: 5 L/min.

column1: How much can cardiac output increase according to the chapter?
column2: Up to approximately six times resting output.

column1: What is the cardiac output formula?
column2: CO = heart rate × stroke volume.

column1: Stroke Volume
column2: The volume of blood ejected by the left ventricle with each contraction.

column1: What controls intrinsic heart rate through automaticity?
column2: The sinoatrial (SA) node.

column1: What is the effect of the brainstem cardioexcitatory center?
column2: Increased sympathetic and decreased parasympathetic activity, increasing heart rate.

column1: What is the effect of the brainstem cardioinhibitory center?
column2: Increased parasympathetic and decreased sympathetic activity, reducing heart rate.

column1: What adrenal hormones contribute to sustained increases in heart rate?
column2: Epinephrine and norepinephrine through beta-1 effects.

column1: Why can excessively fast heart rates decrease cardiac output?
column2: They shorten ventricular filling time, decreasing preload and stroke volume.

column1: What illustrative adult heart rate is associated with reduced filling in the chapter?
column2: Greater than 160 beats/min; not an absolute threshold because age, rhythm, preload and myocardial function matter.

column1: What are the three principal determinants of stroke volume?
column2: Preload, myocardial contractility and afterload.

column1: Preload
column2: End-diastolic myocardial stretch; ventricular end-diastolic pressure and volume are imperfect surrogates.

column1: What is a major determinant of preload?
column2: Venous return.

column1: Frank-Starling Law Of The Heart
column2: Greater end-diastolic myocardial fiber stretch produces a stronger contraction up to a physiological limit.

column1: Why does increasing preload not always increase cardiac output?
column2: Frank–Starling responsiveness is limited; severely dilated or failing ventricles may not respond beneficially.

column1: Myocardial contractility
column2: The force of ventricular contraction.

column1: What factors can reduce myocardial contractility according to the chapter?
column2: Congestive heart failure, myocardial necrosis from infarction and beta-1 blockers.

column1: Afterload
column2: The load opposing ventricular ejection that the ventricle must overcome to eject blood.

column1: Is afterload simply the diastolic blood pressure?
column2: No; diastolic pressure and aortic resistance relate to afterload but do not define it alone.

column1: What can chronically increased afterload contribute to?
column2: Left ventricular failure.

column1: Systemic Vascular Resistance (SVR)
column2: Resistance to systemic blood flow, strongly influenced by vessel diameter.

column1: How does vasoconstriction affect SVR and diastolic pressure?
column2: Smaller vessel diameter increases SVR and tends to increase diastolic pressure.

column1: How does vasodilation affect SVR and diastolic pressure?
column2: Larger vessel diameter decreases SVR and tends to lower diastolic pressure.

column1: What autonomic mechanism promotes systemic vasoconstriction in the chapter?
column2: Sympathetic stimulation through alpha-1 effects.

column1: What mechanisms explain much systemic vasodilation?
column2: Reduced sympathetic tone, local mediators and circulating factors rather than a universal parasympathetic vasodilator response.

column1: Why is diastolic BP not a direct measurement of SVR?
column2: It also depends on arterial compliance, heart rate and arterial runoff.

column1: How does compensatory vasoconstriction during hemorrhage trade pressure for perfusion?
column2: It may preserve arterial pressure while reducing peripheral cellular blood flow.

column1: What findings may reflect reduced peripheral perfusion during blood loss?
column2: Cool skin, weak peripheral pulses and altered mental status.

column1: Why may a patient become quiet or sleepy as cellular perfusion declines?
column2: Inadequate oxygen and energy delivery can impair cellular function and mental status; hypoxia may also produce agitation, so interpret behavior with the full examination.

column1: Pulse Pressure (PP)
column2: The difference between systolic and diastolic blood pressure, expressed in mmHg.

column1: What is the formula for pulse pressure?
column2: Systolic BP − diastolic BP.

column1: What threshold illustrates narrow pulse pressure in the chapter?
column2: Less than 25% of systolic BP; interpret with other clinical findings.

column1: What is the pulse pressure for BP 108/88 mmHg?
column2: 20 mmHg.

column1: Is a BP of 108/88 mmHg a narrow pulse pressure under the chapter's criterion?
column2: Yes. 20 mmHg is less than 25% of 108 (27 mmHg).

column1: What physiological combination may produce narrow pulse pressure during blood loss?
column2: Falling preload and cardiac output lower systolic pressure while compensatory vasoconstriction raises or maintains diastolic pressure.

column1: What pulse quality can accompany narrow pulse pressure?
column2: A weak or thready pulse.

column1: Does narrow pulse pressure alone diagnose hemorrhage?
column2: No; interpret trends and the entire examination.

column1: Microcirculation
column2: Blood flow through arterioles, capillaries and venules where gases, nutrients and wastes are exchanged with cells.

column1: What is the microvascular flow sequence in the chapter?
column2: Arterioles → metarterioles → true capillaries → venules.

column1: Metarterioles
column2: Thoroughfare pathways within the microcirculation.

column1: What is the primary function of true capillaries?
column2: Exchange of gases, nutrients and wastes.

column1: How do precapillary sphincters regulate local capillary perfusion?
column2: Relaxation opens capillaries; contraction shunts blood away.

column1: What are the three regulatory influences on microcirculation?
column2: Local, neural and hormonal factors.

column1: Which factors dominate microcirculatory regulation at rest in the chapter?
column2: Local factors.

column1: What local factors affect microcirculation?
column2: Temperature, hypoxia, acidosis and histamine.

column1: How does sympathetic activity affect precapillary sphincters in the chapter?
column2: It promotes constriction and closure.

column1: Is parasympathetic dilation the general counterpart of sympathetic constriction in systemic vessels?
column2: No; local metabolic and endothelial signals, circulating hormones and sympathetic tone regulate most systemic vascular flow.

column1: What hormone provides a sustained constricting effect on microcirculation in the chapter?
column2: Epinephrine through alpha-1 effects.

column1: Does an adequate measured blood pressure prove adequate microcirculatory perfusion?
column2: No; arterial pressure does not directly establish capillary-level exchange.

column1: What clinical findings help an EMT assess changes in peripheral perfusion?
column2: Serial skin temperature and color, peripheral pulses, mental status and capillary refill when appropriate; no single finding establishes adequate perfusion.

column1: What is the chapter's simplified relationship between blood pressure, cardiac output and systemic vascular resistance?
column2: BP ≈ CO × SVR; a conceptual relationship, not a direct systolic or diastolic pressure calculation.

column1: Baroreceptors
column2: Stretch-sensitive pressure receptors in the aortic arch and carotid sinuses that signal changes in arterial pressure.

column1: Where do baroreceptors send signals to regulate blood pressure?
column2: The medulla's cardioregulatory and vasomotor centers.

column1: What happens to baroreceptor stretch and firing when blood pressure rises?
column2: Both increase.

column1: How does the autonomic nervous system respond to increased baroreceptor firing?
column2: Parasympathetic activity increases and sympathetic activity decreases.

column1: How does the baroreflex reduce blood pressure when it rises?
column2: Reduces heart rate and contractility, promotes vasodilation and reduces SVR and venous return.

column1: What happens to baroreceptor stretch and firing when blood pressure falls?
column2: Both decrease.

column1: How does the autonomic nervous system respond to decreased baroreceptor firing?
column2: Sympathetic activity increases and parasympathetic activity decreases.

column1: How does the baroreflex compensate for falling blood pressure?
column2: Increases heart rate and contractility and promotes vasoconstriction, raising SVR and venous return/preload.

column1: Which adrenal hormones are released in response to a significant BP drop?
column2: Epinephrine and norepinephrine.

column1: What receptor actions of epinephrine are listed in the chapter's pressure regulation discussion?
column2: Alpha-1, alpha-2 and beta-1 effects.

column1: What receptor actions of norepinephrine are identified by the chapter and its clarification?
column2: Alpha-1, alpha-2 and beta-1 effects.

column1: What chemoreceptor stimuli activate the medulla's cardioexcitatory and vasomotor centers?
column2: A significant fall in arterial oxygen with increased CO₂ and decreased pH.

column1: What cardiovascular response can chemoreceptor stimulation produce during hypoxia?
column2: Increased heart rate, contractility and vasoconstriction.

column1: Why may hypoxia present with pale, cool skin and tachycardia?
column2: Chemoreceptor-mediated sympathetic responses increase heart rate and constrict peripheral vessels.

column1: Why can blood pressure remain apparently acceptable during worsening hemorrhagic shock?
column2: Baroreflex compensation maintains pressure despite declining cardiac output and tissue perfusion.

column1: In the chapter's penetrating abdominal trauma case, what scene hazard had to be controlled even after police secured the scene?
column2: An aggressive dog had to be secured before care proceeded.

column1: In penetrating abdominal trauma, what do moaning and answering questions establish about the airway?
column2: It is open with some air movement at that moment, but adequate alveolar ventilation is not established.

column1: In the chapter's abdominal trauma case, why does a rate of 24/min with shallow breaths and visible chest rise not establish adequate alveolar ventilation?
column2: Tidal volume is uncertain, and visible chest rise does not quantify effective alveolar ventilation.

column1: Which abdominal findings in penetrating trauma raise concern for internal hemorrhage?
column2: Severe abdominal pain, rigidity and tenderness.

column1: What clinical findings in the chapter's internal hemorrhage case indicate poor perfusion?
column2: Barely palpable radial pulse, pale cool clammy skin, HR 122/min and narrow pulse pressure with suspected internal blood loss.

column1: What is the pulse pressure for BP 102/88 mmHg?
column2: 14 mmHg.

column1: Does BP 102/88 mmHg meet the chapter's narrow pulse pressure example?
column2: Yes. 14 mmHg is less than 25% of systolic BP (25.5 mmHg).

column1: Why was a nonrebreather at 15 L/min used in the chapter's internal hemorrhage scenario?
column2: To increase alveolar oxygen availability and binding to available hemoglobin; this is illustrative, not a universal prescription.

column1: How does internal hemorrhage reduce stroke volume and cardiac output?
column2: Blood loss reduces venous return and preload, reducing ventricular filling and stroke volume.

column1: Why is tachycardia compensatory in the abdominal hemorrhage case?
column2: An increased heart rate attempts to maintain cardiac output despite falling stroke volume.

column1: Why is the patient with internal hemorrhage pale, cool and clammy with a weak radial pulse?
column2: Sympathetic vasoconstriction redirects blood flow away from the periphery as the body compensates for blood loss.

column1: Why is a systolic pressure of 102 mmHg not reassuring in the chapter's abdominal hemorrhage case?
column2: The narrow pulse pressure, weak pulse, skin findings and suspected internal bleeding indicate compromised perfusion despite compensation.

column1: Can covering penetrating abdominal wounds stop internal hemorrhage?
column2: No; internal bleeding requires definitive management.

column1: What BLS care is indicated in the chapter's suspected internal hemorrhage case?
column2: Maintain scene safety, cover wounds appropriately, assess ABCs, control external bleeding, support oxygenation and ventilation as indicated, limit heat loss and expedite trauma transport.

column1: How should ALS intercept be handled during suspected internal hemorrhage?
column2: Request ALS according to local intercept policy without delaying definitive care.

column1: What should occur during transport of a patient with suspected internal hemorrhage?
column2: Reassess en route, communicate deterioration and notify the receiving facility early.

column1: What is required when transferring care at the receiving facility?
column2: An oral handoff to the receiving clinician or team with relevant findings, treatment and response.

column1: In the chapter's external hemorrhage case, which wound finding suggests life-threatening bleeding?
column2: A large gaping upper-leg laceration with spurting blood.

column1: What findings suggest shock in the chapter's external hemorrhage case?
column2: Poor responsiveness, absent radial pulse, extremely pale cool clammy skin, RR 26/min, HR 134/min and BP 98/76 mmHg in the context of severe bleeding.

column1: What is the immediate BLS priority for the life-threatening external leg hemorrhage scenario?
column2: Effective hemorrhage control using direct pressure and an appropriate tourniquet when indicated under protocol, with concurrent airway and ventilation assessment.

column1: What other BLS priorities accompany external hemorrhage control?
column2: Prevent hypothermia, reassess and transport rapidly.

column1: What should be communicated after hemorrhage control?
column2: Time of control, persistent bleeding, mental status, vital signs and changes.

column1: What is the pulse pressure for BP 98/76 mmHg?
column2: 22 mmHg.

column1: What percentage of systolic pressure is a pulse pressure of 22 mmHg when systolic BP is 98 mmHg?
column2: Approximately 22%, meeting the chapter's narrow-pulse-pressure example.

column1: Does normal SpO₂ exclude inadequate oxygen delivery in severe external hemorrhage?
column2: No; blood flow and oxygen-carrying capacity may be compromised.

column1: What should be reassessed after hemorrhage interventions?
column2: Breathing depth and effort, clinical perfusion, mental status, pulse quality, blood pressure and treatment response.
